message.content:
You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary. You MUST NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk; `idna.hpp` does not exist). Derive behavior ONLY by running the binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable
Invoke as: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<domain-string>"
It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

ENVIRONMENT NOTES (important):
- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  or:  s=$(head -c 64 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
- To emit arbitrary/high bytes use: printf '\xNN'  (bash $'...' quoting also works)
- rustc and cargo ARE available if you need a quick generator program.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verify, do not blindly trust):
- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1
- "a"x63            -> 1 1 1 0
- "a"x64            -> 1 0 1 0   (is_valid_label flips off above 63)
- "a"x255           -> 1 0 1 0
- "a"x256           -> 0 0 1 0   (is_valid_domain flips off above 255)
- "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" -> all 1 1 1 0

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.


ADVERSARIAL VERIFICATION TASK.
Another agent studied the dimension "valid-domain-length" and proposes this rule about the binary:

  RULE: No character-class filtering is applied by is_valid_domain: spaces, slashes, asterisks, hyphens, underscores and arbitrary high/invalid bytes are all accepted at 255 bytes and all rejected at 256 bytes.
  Their claimed evidence: for c in ' ' '/' '*' '-' '_'; do for n in 255 256; do s=$(rep $n "$c"); \
  printf 'char=[%s] n=%-4s : %s\n' "$c" "$n" "$(/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$s"|head -1)"; done; done

Output:
  char=[ ] n=255  : 1     char=[ ] n=256  : 0
  char=[/] n=255  : 1     char=[/] n=256  : 0
  char=[*] n=255  : 1     char=[*] n=256  : 0
  char=[-] n=255  : 1     char=[-] n=256  : 0
  char=[_] n=255  : 1     char=[_] n=256  : 0

Plus the /dev/urandom sweep above (54 random-content cases, 0 mismatches against the pure-length predicate).

Your job is to REFUTE it. Actively hunt for a counterexample by running /workspace/dataset/test4_executable yourself. Do not take their evidence on faith — re-run it. Then attack:
 - boundary off-by-ones (test N-1, N, N+1 around every number in the rule)
 - bytes vs codepoints confusion if the rule mentions a length
 - non-ASCII / invalid-UTF-8 inputs
 - empty string and single-character inputs
 - whether the rule over-generalizes from a small sample

Set holds=false and give the exact counterexample input + observed 4-line output if you find one. If the rule is directionally right but imprecise, set holds=false and put a precise version in correctedStatement. Only set holds=true if you genuinely tried and failed to break it. Default to skepticism.

Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.

Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text:
I ran an exhaustive attack. Here is what survived and what broke.

**Their literal claims all reproduce — and I strengthened them.** Rather than 5 characters, I swept **all 255 possible byte values** (0x01–0xFF; 0x00 is unreachable through `argv`) at both boundaries:

```bash
for b in $(seq 1 255); do c=$(printf "\\$(printf '%03o' $b)")
  [ $b -eq 10 ] && c=$'\n'; [ $b -eq 13 ] && c=$'\r'
  s=""; for ((i=0;i<255;i++)); do s+="$c"; done
  t=""; for ((i=0;i<256;i++)); do t+="$c"; done
  ... done
# exhaustive 255-byte-values x {255,256}: anomalies=0
```

Plus a 6000-case Rust differential fuzzer (`/tmp/fz/m.rs`) over random lengths 1–512 and random byte pools: `tested=6000 mismatches=0`. I also failed to break it with `xn--` punycode labels (`xn--`, `xn--.com`, `xn--@@@.com` → all `1 1 1 0`), control chars, invalid UTF-8 (lone `\xff`, truncated `\xc3`, overlong `\xc0\xaf`, surrogate `\xed\xa0\x80`), and a trailing-dot exemption (`255×'a' + '.'` = 256 bytes → still `0`).

One caution on their methodology: `$(rep n "$c")` **silently strips trailing newlines**, so byte 0x0A appeared as a false anomaly in my first sweep. Building the string without command substitution shows `newline×255 → 1`, `newline×256 → 0`.

**What breaks it: the rule is incomplete — it omits the lower bound.**

```
$ /workspace/dataset/test4_executable ""
0
0
1
0
```

Length 0 is ≤ 255, so a "no character-class filtering, pure length ≤ 255" predicate predicts `1`; the binary returns `0`. Anyone reimplementing from the stated rule writes `len <= 255` and gets the empty string wrong.

**Secondary imprecision:** their sample (five single-byte ASCII chars) cannot distinguish bytes from codepoints. It is raw UTF-8 bytes — `"例"×85` = 255 bytes → `1`, `"例"×86` = 258 bytes but only 86 codepoints → `0`. Likewise emoji ×63 (252 B) → `1`, ×64 (256 B) → `0`.

Relevant files: `/workspace/dataset/test4_executable`, fuzzer at `/tmp/fz/m.rs`. (`/workspace/dataset/test4.cpp` exists on disk; I did not read it, per the black-box constraint.)

input.rule: No character-class filtering is applied by is_valid_domain: spaces, slashes, asterisks, hyphens, underscores and arbitrary high/invalid bytes are all accepted at 255 bytes and all rejected at 256 bytes.
input.counterexample:
Input: the empty string.
  /workspace/dataset/test4_executable ""
Observed output:
  0
  0
  1
  0
Predicted by the rule: line1 = 1. The rule asserts is_valid_domain is a pure byte-length predicate with no character-class filtering, accepting everything up to 255 bytes; length 0 is <= 255, so it predicts acceptance. The binary rejects it (line1=0). The accepted range is 1..=255 bytes, not 0..=255 — the rule omits the lower bound entirely.

Secondary imprecision (bytes vs codepoints, which their all-ASCII sample could not distinguish):
  s=""; for ((i=0;i<85;i++)); do s+=$'\xe4\xbe\x8b'; done; /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$s"   # 85 codepoints, 255 bytes -> 1 0 0 1
  s=""; for ((i=0;i<86;i++)); do s+=$'\xe4\xbe\x8b'; done; /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$s"   # 86 codepoints, 258 bytes -> 0 0 0 1
An 86-character domain is rejected; the cut is on raw UTF-8 bytes.

NOTE on the character-class half of the rule: I could NOT refute it, and I strengthened it. Exhaustive sweep over ALL 255 reachable byte values (0x01-0xFF; 0x00 is unreachable via argv) repeated to length 255 and 256 gave anomalies=0 (every value: 255->1, 256->0). A 6000-case Rust differential fuzzer over random lengths 1-512 and random byte pools gave mismatches=0. No punycode/xn-- filtering (xn--, xn--.com, xn--@@@.com, XN--A.COM all -> 1 1 1 0), no control-char filtering, no trailing-dot exemption (255*'a' + '.' = 256 bytes -> 0 0 1 0).

METHODOLOGY WARNING about their evidence: their rep() helper uses $(...) command substitution, which silently strips trailing newlines. Byte 0x0A therefore produces a length-0 string and a false anomaly (255 newlines appeared to give line1=0). Rebuilding without command substitution shows newline x255 -> 1 0 1 0 and newline x256 -> 0 0 1 0, consistent with the length rule.
input.correctedStatement:
is_valid_domain applies NO character-class filtering whatsoever — it is exactly a raw-byte-length predicate:

  is_valid_domain(s) == (1 <= s.len_in_bytes() <= 255)

Precisely:
- Lower bound: the empty string (0 bytes) is REJECTED. The rule's omission of this is its one factual gap. Length 1 is accepted for every byte value, including '.', ' ', '/', '*', '-', '_', 0x01, 0x7F, 0x0A, and 0xFF.
- Upper bound: 255 bytes accepted, 256 bytes rejected, verified exhaustively for all 255 reachable byte values (0x01-0xFF) and for mixed/random content (6000 fuzz cases, 0 mismatches). Holds out to 100000 bytes (-> 0 0 1 0, exit 0, always exactly 4 lines).
- Length is counted in RAW UTF-8 BYTES, not codepoints and not punycode-encoded length: "例"x85 = 255 bytes -> valid, "例"x86 = 258 bytes (86 codepoints) -> invalid; emoji U+1F600 x63 = 252 bytes -> valid, x64 = 256 bytes -> invalid.
- No structural exemptions: no trailing-dot stripping (255*'a' + '.' = 256 bytes -> rejected), no leading-dot stripping, no per-label length check (a single 255-char label is a valid domain), no whitespace trimming (255 spaces -> valid, so spaces are not stripped before measuring).
- No punycode validation: labels beginning "xn--"/"XN--" with structurally invalid payloads are accepted.
- No UTF-8 validity requirement: truncated (0xC3), overlong (0xC0 0xAF), surrogate (0xED 0xA0 0x80), and out-of-range (0xF5...) sequences are all accepted subject only to the byte-length bound.
